topic: Why does time feel faster as you get older?
research_summary: Channel check: NOT AVAILABLE: the YouTube sign-in has no read scopes yet (data/channel_trends.json says 'insufficient authentication scopes'); vidIQ shows only public totals (47 subscribers, 11,241 views, 140 videos) and has 3 credits, so there is no per-video data. No change was made because of channel data; the variety guard decided (Space and Earth & Nature are cooling down). Candidates: (1) Why does time feel faster as you get older? 34/40 (universal, shareable, evergreen, memory-and-novelty angle with a practical fix, simple visuals), (2) Why do we forget our dreams so fast? 31, (3) How does Google Maps know about traffic jams? 30 (continues the GPS cluster but less universal). Winner: the time question; continues the open 'Mind Glitches' follow-ups (deja vu video). Titles (/50): 'Why Does Time Feel Faster as You Get Older?' 45 (chosen); 'Why Do Years Fly By as You Age?' 42; 'Why Summer Felt Endless as a Kid' 40; 'Your Brain Is Shrinking Your Years' 38; 'The Memory Trick Behind Fast Years' 37; 'Why Is Every Year Shorter?' 36; 'How to Slow Down Time (Science)' 39; 'Why 40 Feels Faster Than 8' 36; 'Time Speeds Up: Here Is Why' 38; 'Why Weeks Vanish' 30. Thumbnails: A the face with a clock racing and the words 'Why does time speed up?' (chosen); B a calendar with pages flying; C a child and an adult with the same clock. Hooks: 'A year felt endless at eight. Now one disappears in a blink.' (chosen); 'You are not imagining it: years really do feel shorter.'; 'Your childhood summers were not longer. Your memories were.'; 'One experiment asked five hundred people how fast a decade felt.'; 'The same year, two different lengths.' Gap: most existing videos give only the 'a year is a smaller fraction of your life' story or the novelty story; this one sets the two side by side (flagging the first as unproven), explains the holiday effect with the same mechanism, cites the age survey, and ends with a practical test (try one new thing). Claims: (1) Wittmann and Lehnhoff 2005 surveyed 499 people aged 14 to 94; short intervals did not feel faster with age, but a decade did for older people - sources: Scientific American, University of Geneva archive - PARTIALLY VERIFIED (press coverage of the paper; one account says the effect was weaker, so the script says 'felt faster to the older ones'); (2) novelty builds more memories and routine fewer, so busy same-again years look short in hindsight - Wittmann, Hammond - PARTIALLY VERIFIED hypothesis, stated as 'Theory two'; (3) a year is a smaller fraction of life as you age (Janet's ratio idea, 1877) - an old idea, NOT proven, stated as 'never proven'; (4) holiday effect: trips feel long in hindsight because of many new memories (Hammond, 'Time Warped') - PARTIALLY VERIFIED, the 6-9 memories per day figure comes from a conference report so it is left out; (5) Bejan 2019 mental-image-rate model - no independent test found, LEFT OUT. Sources: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-does-time-seem-to-speed-up-with-age/ , https://www.psychologicalscience.org/observer/vacation-not-what-you-remember , https://www.npr.org/sections/krulwich/2010/02/01/122322542/why-does-time-fly-by-as-you-get-older . Competitor/vidIQ data: NOT PUBLICLY VERIFIABLE. Risks: the age survey effect is modest and sources differ (hedged); 'practical fix' is a suggestion, not medical advice. Quality gate 84/100: topic 9, curiosity 9, title 8, thumbnail 8, opening 9, story 8, visual 8, emotion 8, retention 8, series 8 - improve the visuals of the survey scene, then proceed.

scenes.text: A year felt endless at eight. Now one disappears in a blink.
In this video you'll see two old theories, a memory trick, and how to slow your years down. Ready?
Theory one: a year is an eighth of an eight-year-old's life, but a fortieth at forty. An old idea, never proven.

graphic.headline: One year as a share of life

scenes.text: Theory two: novelty. New things build strong memories; routine leaves almost none. So same-again years look short.
That is the holiday effect. Why do trips feel long afterwards? They are packed with firsts.
A survey of nearly five hundred people, aged fourteen to ninety-four: a decade felt faster to the older ones.
Quick quiz. Which year feels longer afterwards: a routine one, or one full of firsts? Firsts.
So stretch your years: try one new thing this week. What will you try first? Tell me below!
